chapter: Ch 3 — The Sale of Goods Act, 1930

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT 'goods' within the meaning of section 2(7) of the Sale of Goods Act 1930?

readLink.label: Read: Meaning of goods, s. 2(7) →

options.text: Equity shares of a listed company
options.explanation: This forgets that stock and shares are expressly named in s. 2(7) as included in goods, however unlike ordinary movables they seem.

options.text: Standing timber agreed to be severed before sale
options.explanation: Things attached to the land which are agreed to be severed before sale or under the contract of sale are expressly included by s. 2(7).

options.text: A debt owed to the seller by a third party
options.explanation: Correct. A debt is an actionable claim, and s. 2(7) expressly excludes actionable claims from the definition of goods.

options.text: Old silver coins sold to a collector for their rarity
options.explanation: Money is excluded only as currency; coins sold as collectors' items are ordinary movable property and therefore goods.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 4 · Essentials of a contract of sale
questions.stem: Ramesh transfers his motorcycle to Suresh and takes in exchange Suresh's refrigerator of the same value. No money changes hands. The transaction is:

readLink.label: Read: Sale and agreement to sell, s. 4 →

options.text: An exchange or barter, to which the Sale of Goods Act 1930 does not apply
options.explanation: Correct. A sale requires a money consideration (the 'price', s. 2(10)); goods given for goods is barter, governed by the general law of contract.

options.text: A sale, because property in goods has passed for consideration
options.explanation: This treats any consideration as sufficient; s. 4(1) read with s. 2(10) requires the consideration to be money.

options.text: An agreement to sell, since no price has yet been fixed
options.explanation: This misdiagnoses the defect as a missing price term. No price can ever be fixed here because the consideration is goods, not money.

options.text: A bailment, because possession of each article has changed hands
options.explanation: In a bailment ownership never moves and the goods must come back; here ownership of each article has passed outright.

questions.stem: For the purposes of the Sale of Goods Act 1930, a person is 'insolvent' when:

readLink.label: Read: Where this Act sits, s. 2(8) →

options.text: A court has adjudged him insolvent on a petition by his creditors
options.explanation: This reads an adjudication requirement into s. 2(8) that the section deliberately excludes with the words 'whether he has committed an act of insolvency or not'.

options.text: His liabilities exceed his assets on a balance-sheet test
options.explanation: The Act uses a cash-flow test about paying debts as they fall due, not a balance-sheet comparison of assets and liabilities.

options.text: He has defaulted on a single payment to any one creditor
options.explanation: One default is not a cessation of payment in the ordinary course of business; the section looks at the pattern, not an isolated failure.

options.text: He has ceased to pay his debts in the ordinary course of business, or cannot pay them as they become due, whether or not he has been adjudged insolvent
options.explanation: Correct. Section 2(8) uses this commercial test and expressly makes adjudication irrelevant, which is what lets an unpaid seller stop goods in transit quickly.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 4(3) · Sale versus agreement to sell
questions.stem: The single test that distinguishes a 'sale' from an 'agreement to sell' under section 4(3) is:

readLink.label: Read: Sale and agreement to sell, s. 4 →

options.text: Whether the price has been paid in full
options.explanation: Payment is irrelevant to the classification. Section 20 says expressly that postponing the time of payment does not stop the property passing.

options.text: Whether the property in the goods has passed to the buyer or is still to pass
options.explanation: Correct. Section 4(3) turns entirely on the moment of transfer of property; everything else, including payment and delivery, is beside the point.

options.text: Whether the goods have been physically delivered to the buyer
options.explanation: Delivery is a transfer of possession (s. 2(2)); the classification depends on the transfer of ownership, which may happen without any delivery.

options.text: Whether the contract has been reduced to writing and signed
options.explanation: The Act requires no writing at all; a contract of sale may be made orally or be implied from conduct.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 4 · Consequences of the distinction
questions.stem: Anil agrees to sell his lathe to Bhaskar, property to pass on payment of the last instalment. Before that instalment falls due Anil is adjudged insolvent, though Bhaskar has already paid 80 per cent of the price. Bhaskar may:

readLink.label: Read: Sale and agreement to sell, s. 4 →

options.text: Only prove in the insolvency as an ordinary creditor for the money he has paid
options.explanation: Correct. This is an agreement to sell, so the lathe still belongs to Anil and vests in the Official Assignee; Bhaskar has a personal claim for a dividend, not a claim to the goods.

options.text: Claim the lathe from the Official Assignee, having paid most of the price
options.explanation: Payment of most of the price does not transfer ownership. Only a completed transfer of property would let him claim the goods themselves.

options.text: Claim the lathe on tendering the balance instalment to the Official Assignee
options.explanation: A tender now cannot resurrect a contract whose subject matter has vested in the estate; his remedy sounds in money.

options.text: Sue the Official Assignee for specific performance as of right
options.explanation: Specific performance under s. 58 is discretionary and is not available as of right, least of all against an insolvent estate.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 4 · Consequences of the distinction
questions.stem: Where there is a SALE and the seller, still in possession, wrongfully resells the same goods to an innocent third party, the general position of that third party is that:

readLink.label: Read: Transfer of title by a non-owner →

options.text: He always gets a good title, because possession is nine points of the law
options.explanation: Possession is not a source of title in Indian law; the third party is protected by a specific statutory exception, not by a maxim.

options.text: He never gets any title, because the seller had already parted with ownership
options.explanation: This applies s. 27 without its exceptions. Section 30(1) exists precisely to protect this buyer.

options.text: He may nevertheless get a good title, because s. 30(1) protects a buyer in good faith from a seller left in possession
options.explanation: Correct. The nemo dat rule would give him nothing, but s. 30(1) is an express statutory exception for a seller continuing in possession after a sale, provided the third party takes in good faith and without notice.

options.text: He gets a good title only if he has also paid the full price in cash
options.explanation: Section 30(1) speaks of good faith and want of notice, not of the mode or completeness of payment.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 4 · Nature of the right
questions.stem: Which pairing is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Sale and agreement to sell, s. 4 →

options.text: Sale — right in personam; agreement to sell — right in rem
options.explanation: This reverses the two. An owner has the right against the world, not the person who is merely promised ownership.

options.text: Sale — right in rem; agreement to sell — right in personam
options.explanation: Correct. Once property passes the buyer has a proprietary right good against the world; before it passes he has only a contractual claim against the seller.

options.text: Both create a right in rem from the date of the contract
options.explanation: An agreement to sell creates no proprietary right at all until the property passes under s. 4(4).

options.text: Both create only a right in personam until delivery
options.explanation: This makes delivery the decisive event. Property, not delivery, converts the buyer's right into a right in rem.

questions.stem: Which feature belongs to a hire-purchase agreement and NOT to a sale of goods payable by instalments?

readLink.label: Read: Sale distinguished from its neighbours →

options.text: Possession of the goods passes to the person in possession at the start
options.explanation: Possession passes at the start in both; it is ownership that behaves differently.

options.text: The instalments are fixed in advance and paid periodically
options.explanation: Periodic fixed instalments are common to both arrangements and decide nothing.

options.text: A third party buying from the person in possession in good faith gets a good title
options.explanation: This is true of an instalment SALE and false of hire-purchase, where the hirer has not agreed to buy and so falls outside s. 30(2).

options.text: The person in possession may return the goods at any time and refuse to pay the remaining instalments
options.explanation: Correct. The hirer is a bailee with an option to purchase; he is never bound to complete, whereas an instalment buyer owes the whole price from the outset.

questions.stem: Kavita commissions a well-known artist to paint her portrait on his own canvas for ₹2,00,000. The contract is best classified as:

readLink.label: Read: Sale distinguished from its neighbours →

options.text: A sale of goods, because a chattel is delivered for a money price
options.explanation: This applies the form rather than the substance. Delivery of a chattel is incidental here; what is bought is the artist's skill.

options.text: An agreement to sell future goods under s. 6(3)
options.explanation: The classification question comes first. If the contract is not one of sale at all, the future-goods rule never arises.

options.text: A bailment of the canvas and paints
options.explanation: Nothing of Kavita's is entrusted to the artist; he uses his own materials, so there is no bailment.

options.text: A contract for work and materials, because the substance of the bargain is the artist's skill
options.explanation: Correct. Where the essence is the exercise of skill and labour and the material is merely incidental, the contract is one for work and materials, not a sale of goods.

questions.stem: Farid agrees in March to sell Gita 40 quintals of the mangoes his orchard will produce in June. The contract is:

readLink.label: Read: Kinds of goods and goods that perish →

options.text: A sale of specific goods, the orchard being identified
options.explanation: The orchard is identified but the goods are not; specific goods must be identified and agreed upon at the time the contract is made (s. 2(14)).

options.text: An agreement to sell future goods, which cannot operate as a sale however the parties describe it
options.explanation: Correct. The mangoes are goods to be produced after the contract, so s. 6(3) makes the contract operate only as an agreement to sell.

options.text: A contract for contingent goods under s. 6(2)
options.explanation: Contingent goods depend on a contingency which may or may not happen. A normal crop from the seller's own orchard is future, not contingent.

options.text: Void, because the seller does not own the goods at the date of the contract
options.explanation: Not owning the goods yet is exactly the situation s. 6(3) provides for; it makes the contract an agreement to sell, not a nullity.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · ss. 7 and 8 · Perishing of goods
questions.stem: A consignment of specific goods lying in a warehouse is destroyed by fire two days BEFORE the contract of sale is made, and neither party knows of the fire when they contract. The contract is:

readLink.label: Read: Kinds of goods and goods that perish →

options.text: Void under section 7
options.explanation: Correct. Specific goods that had perished before the contract was made, without the seller's knowledge, make the contract void under s. 7 — the goods-based form of bilateral mistake.

options.text: Voidable at the option of the buyer
options.explanation: Voidability belongs to defective consent under ss. 19 and 19A of the Contract Act; a common mistake about the very existence of the subject matter makes the agreement void, not voidable.

options.text: Avoided under section 8
options.explanation: Section 8 applies to an agreement to sell where the goods perish AFTER the agreement but before risk passes. Here they had already perished.

options.text: Valid, the loss falling on whoever bore the risk at the time of the fire
options.explanation: There can be no allocation of risk in a contract that never came into existence for want of subject matter.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT required for section 8 to avoid an agreement to sell?

readLink.label: Read: Kinds of goods and goods that perish →

options.text: That the goods be specific goods
options.explanation: This IS required. Section 8 applies only to an agreement to sell specific goods, never to generic goods.

options.text: That the goods perish without any fault of the seller or the buyer
options.explanation: This IS required. Fault on either side takes the case out of s. 8 and into ordinary breach.

options.text: That the buyer should have paid at least part of the price
options.explanation: Correct. Section 8 says nothing about payment; it requires specific goods, perishing without the fault of either party, and that this happen before the risk passes to the buyer.

options.text: That the perishing occur before the risk has passed to the buyer
options.explanation: This IS required, and it is the limb that most often decides the answer, because risk normally travels with property.

questions.stem: A contract of sale is made without any mention of the price and without any past dealings between the parties. The contract is:

readLink.label: Read: The price, ss. 9 to 11 →

options.text: Void for uncertainty under s. 29 of the Indian Contract Act
options.explanation: Section 9 is a statutory cure for exactly this uncertainty, so the general rule about uncertain agreements does not apply.

options.text: Valid; the buyer must pay a reasonable price, which is a question of fact in each case
options.explanation: Correct. Section 9(2) supplies a reasonable price where the price is not fixed by the contract, by an agreed manner or by the course of dealing, and expressly makes reasonableness a question of fact.

options.text: Valid, the price being the market price on the date of delivery
options.explanation: A reasonable price often resembles the market price but the Act does not equate the two; the market price is only evidence.

options.text: An agreement to sell only, until a price is fixed
options.explanation: The classification in s. 4(3) depends on the passing of property, not on whether the price has been quantified.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 10 · Agreement to sell at valuation
questions.stem: Goods are agreed to be sold at a price to be fixed by a valuer, who refuses to act. Part of the goods has already been delivered to and appropriated by the buyer. The correct position is:

readLink.label: Read: The price, ss. 9 to 11 →

options.text: The agreement is avoided and the buyer may keep the delivered goods without payment
options.explanation: This ignores the express proviso to s. 10(1), which exists to prevent exactly that windfall.

options.text: The agreement stands and the court will fix the price
options.explanation: Section 10 avoids the agreement where the third party cannot or does not make the valuation; it does not transfer the valuation to the court.

options.text: The agreement stands and the buyer must pay the market price for all the goods
options.explanation: There is no statutory substitution of the market price, and the agreement does not survive the valuer's failure.

options.text: The agreement is avoided, but the buyer must pay a reasonable price for the goods he has appropriated
options.explanation: Correct. Section 10(1) avoids the agreement and its proviso requires payment of a reasonable price for goods delivered to and appropriated by the buyer.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 11 · Stipulations as to time
questions.stem: Under section 11, unless a different intention appears from the terms of the contract:

readLink.label: Read: The price, ss. 9 to 11 →

options.text: No stipulation as to time is ever of the essence of a contract of sale
options.explanation: This over-reads the section. Time of delivery is ordinarily of the essence in a commercial sale, and the section leaves other time stipulations to be construed.

options.text: Stipulations as to the time of delivery are not deemed to be of the essence
options.explanation: This swaps delivery for payment; the presumption in s. 11 runs the other way for delivery.

options.text: Stipulations as to the time of payment are not deemed to be of the essence of a contract of sale
options.explanation: Correct. Section 11 creates that presumption for the time of PAYMENT only, leaving every other time stipulation to the terms of the contract.

options.text: Every stipulation as to time is of the essence unless the contract says otherwise
options.explanation: This inverts the presumption the section actually creates for the time of payment.

questions.stem: Devyani contracts to buy 800 kg of cardamom from Elango at ₹1,450 per kg. Elango delivers only 620 kg and Devyani, who needs the spice at once, accepts the short delivery. The amount she is bound to pay for what she has received is:

readLink.label: Read: Delivery of the wrong quantity, s. 37 →

options.explanation: Correct. Where the buyer accepts a short delivery she must pay for the goods delivered at the CONTRACT rate: 620 kg × ₹1,450 = ₹8,99,000. Her claim for the shortfall is a separate action for damages.
This charges her for the full contracted 800 kg × ₹1,450 even though only 620 kg was delivered; s. 37(1) makes her pay only for what she accepts.
This is the value of the 180 kg NOT delivered, which is the base for her damages claim, not the amount she owes.

options.text: Nothing until the balance 180 kg is delivered
options.explanation: Section 37(1) gave her the choice of rejecting the whole; having accepted the short delivery she must pay at the contract rate for it.

questions.stem: A term described in the written contract as a 'warranty' turns out, on construction, to go to the very root of the bargain. Under section 12(4) it is:

readLink.label: Read: Conditions and warranties, ss. 12 and 13 →

options.text: A warranty, because the parties are free to agree how their terms are classified
options.explanation: Freedom of contract does not extend to relabelling a term so as to change the remedy; s. 12(4) makes construction decisive.

options.text: Void for inconsistency with the Act
options.explanation: There is no inconsistency to strike down; the section simply construes the term according to its substance.

options.text: A condition, because whether a stipulation is a condition or a warranty depends on the construction of the contract and not on the name given to it
options.explanation: Correct. Section 12(4) says in terms that a stipulation may be a condition though called a warranty in the contract.

options.text: A condition only if the buyer has not yet accepted the goods
options.explanation: Acceptance affects the REMEDY under s. 13(2); it does not change the classification of the term.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 13(2) · Breach of condition treated as breach of warranty
questions.stem: A buyer under a non-severable contract has accepted part of the goods and then discovers a breach of condition. He may:

readLink.label: Read: Conditions and warranties, ss. 12 and 13 →

options.text: Reject the whole of the goods and repudiate the contract
options.explanation: The right to reject is precisely what acceptance destroys under s. 13(2).

options.text: Only treat the breach as a breach of warranty and claim damages
options.explanation: Correct. Section 13(2) compulsorily converts the breach into a breach of warranty once the buyer has accepted the goods or part of them under a non-severable contract.

options.text: Reject only the part not yet accepted and keep the rest
options.explanation: That would be the position under a severable contract; the stem says the contract is not severable.

options.text: Claim nothing, having accepted the goods
options.explanation: Acceptance removes the right to reject but leaves the buyer his damages, which he may also set off against the price under s. 59(1)(a).

questions.stem: Section 13(1) allows the buyer, where the contract of sale is subject to a condition to be fulfilled by the seller, to:

readLink.label: Read: Conditions and warranties, ss. 12 and 13 →

options.text: Waive the condition, or elect to treat the breach of the condition as a breach of warranty
options.explanation: Correct. Section 13(1) gives the buyer both choices, and both are voluntary — this is the buyer's own election, unlike the compulsory conversion in s. 13(2).

options.text: Convert a breach of warranty into a breach of condition
options.explanation: The Act allows the traffic in one direction only. A warranty can never be raised to a condition.

options.text: Compel the seller to perform the condition specifically in every case
options.explanation: Specific performance under s. 58 is discretionary and confined to specific or ascertained goods.

options.text: Repudiate the contract even after accepting the goods under a non-severable contract
options.explanation: That is exactly what s. 13(2) forbids once acceptance has occurred.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an implied WARRANTY under the Sale of Goods Act 1930?

readLink.label: Read: Implied conditions and warranties →

options.text: That the seller has a right to sell the goods
options.explanation: Section 14(a) makes the right to sell an implied CONDITION, which is why a breach of it returns the whole price.

options.text: That the goods shall correspond with their description
options.explanation: Correspondence with description is an implied condition under s. 15.

options.text: That the bulk shall correspond with the sample in quality
options.explanation: That is one of the three implied conditions on a sale by sample under s. 17.

options.text: That the buyer shall have and enjoy quiet possession of the goods
options.explanation: Correct. Section 14(b) is one of only two implied warranties in the Act; the other is freedom from undisclosed encumbrances under s. 14(c).

questions.stem: A buyer purchases a car for ₹3,10,000 and uses it for four months, after which the true owner reclaims it because the seller had no title. The buyer may recover:

readLink.label: Read: Implied conditions and warranties →

options.text: The whole ₹3,10,000, with no deduction for the four months' use
options.explanation: Correct. Breach of the implied condition as to the right to sell causes a total failure of consideration, since the buyer contracted for ownership and got none — the rule in Rowland v Divall.

options.text: ₹3,10,000 less a reasonable allowance for use and depreciation
options.explanation: This treats the use as a benefit received under the contract. The buyer bargained for ownership, which he never got, so no allowance is made.

options.text: Damages measured by the difference between the price and the car's value when reclaimed
options.explanation: That measure belongs to a breach of warranty. A breach of s. 14(a) is a breach of condition producing a total failure of consideration.

options.text: Nothing, because he has enjoyed possession of the car
options.explanation: Quiet possession for a time is not what he paid for, and s. 14(b) in any event makes undisturbed possession a separate promise that has also failed.

questions.stem: A buyer walks into a shop and asks for a 'Tarang 5-star inverter air conditioner' by name, saying nothing about his requirements. The unit proves unsuitable for his very large hall. The seller is:

readLink.label: Read: Caveat emptor and its exceptions →

options.text: Liable, because the seller deals in air conditioners and must know what suits a large hall
options.explanation: Dealing in the goods is only one limb of s. 16(1); the buyer must also have made his particular purpose known and relied on the seller's skill.

options.text: Liable under s. 16(2), because the unit is unfit for the buyer's hall
options.explanation: Merchantable quality asks whether the goods are fit for the ORDINARY purpose of such goods, not for this buyer's unusually large hall.

options.text: Liable, because s. 16(4) makes an express order override nothing
options.explanation: Section 16(4) is about an express condition or warranty not negativing an implied one; it has no bearing on the trade-name proviso.

options.text: Not liable, because the proviso to s. 16(1) excludes the implied condition of fitness where a specified article is bought under its patent or trade name
options.explanation: Correct. Ordering by trade name without disclosing a purpose shows that the buyer relied on the name rather than on the seller's skill or judgment, which is what the proviso assumes.

questions.stem: A buyer examines a consignment of tiles and takes delivery. Two months later a latent manufacturing defect, undetectable on any reasonable inspection, causes the tiles to crack. Under section 16(2):

readLink.label: Read: Implied conditions and warranties →

options.text: The implied condition is excluded, because the buyer examined the goods
options.explanation: This reads the proviso as though examination excluded everything; it excludes only the defects that examination ought to have shown.

options.text: The implied condition of merchantable quality is still available, because the proviso excludes only defects which such examination ought to have revealed
options.explanation: Correct. The proviso is limited by its own words to defects a reasonable examination ought to have revealed, so latent defects remain the seller's responsibility.

options.text: The buyer's only remedy is under s. 17 for a latent defect in the sample
options.explanation: Section 17 applies to a sale by sample, which requires a term to that effect in the contract; nothing in the stem says the sale was by sample.

options.text: The buyer must show that he told the seller the particular purpose for the tiles
options.explanation: That is the requirement of s. 16(1) fitness. Merchantable quality under s. 16(2) needs a sale by description by a dealer, not a stated purpose.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the implied conditions in a contract for sale by sample under section 17?

readLink.label: Read: Implied conditions and warranties →

options.text: That the bulk shall correspond with the sample in quality
options.explanation: This IS one of the three conditions expressly stated in s. 17(2)(a).

options.text: That the buyer shall have a reasonable opportunity of comparing the bulk with the sample
options.explanation: This IS one of the three conditions, in s. 17(2)(b).

options.text: That the sample shall be of merchantable quality when it is shown to the buyer
options.explanation: Correct. Section 17 says nothing about the quality of the sample itself; its three conditions concern the bulk corresponding with the sample, a reasonable opportunity to compare, and freedom from latent defects making the goods unmerchantable.

options.text: That the goods shall be free from any defect rendering them unmerchantable which would not be apparent on reasonable examination of the sample
options.explanation: This IS the third condition, in s. 17(2)(c), and it is confined to latent defects.

questions.stem: Tinned fruit is contracted for in cases of 30 tins each. The seller delivers the correct total quantity but packed in cases of 24 tins, the fruit being sound. The buyer:

readLink.label: Read: Implied conditions and warranties →

options.text: Must accept, because the total quantity and the quality are exactly as contracted
options.explanation: Quantity and quality are not the test under s. 15; the goods must answer the DESCRIPTION, and the packing was part of it.

options.text: May claim damages but not reject, the packing being collateral
options.explanation: This demotes an express element of the description to a warranty; s. 15 makes correspondence a condition.

options.text: May reject only if he had not seen the goods before the contract
options.explanation: A sale can be by description even where the buyer has seen the goods, if he relies on words identifying something not apparent on inspection.

options.text: May reject the whole consignment, because the goods do not correspond with the description
options.explanation: Correct. Section 15 makes correspondence with the description an implied condition, and it is strict — sound goods that do not answer the description may be rejected (Re Moore and Landauer).

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an exception to the rule of caveat emptor?

readLink.label: Read: Caveat emptor and its exceptions →

options.text: Goods bought by description from a seller who deals in goods of that description
options.explanation: This IS an exception: s. 16(2) implies a condition of merchantable quality.

options.text: A condition annexed by the usage of a particular trade
options.explanation: This IS an exception, preserved by s. 16(3).

options.text: Sale of a specified article under its patent or trade name where the buyer states no purpose
options.explanation: Correct. That proviso to s. 16(1) is the situation in which caveat emptor CONTINUES to apply; it is an exception to the exception, not an exception to the rule.

options.text: Consent obtained by the seller's active concealment of a defect
options.explanation: This IS an exception; fraud takes the case outside caveat emptor and engages ss. 17 to 19 of the Contract Act.

questions.stem: For the implied condition of fitness for a particular purpose under section 16(1) to arise, which combination is required?

readLink.label: Read: Caveat emptor and its exceptions →

options.text: The purpose is made known expressly or by implication, the buyer relies on the seller's skill or judgment, and the goods are of a description it is in the course of the seller's business to supply
options.explanation: Correct. All three limbs must be present, and whether the seller is the manufacturer or producer is expressly immaterial.

options.text: The purpose is made known, and the seller is the manufacturer of the goods
options.explanation: Section 16(1) says in terms 'whether he be the manufacturer or producer or not', so manufacture is irrelevant.

options.text: The buyer relies on the seller's skill and the goods are sold by sample
options.explanation: A sale by sample engages s. 17, which is a separate route with its own three conditions.

options.text: The goods have only one obvious purpose and the buyer has examined them
options.explanation: A single obvious purpose helps prove that the purpose was made known by implication, but examination is a s. 16(2) matter, not a requirement of s. 16(1).

questions.stem: Under section 18, where there is a contract for the sale of unascertained goods:

readLink.label: Read: Passing of property →

options.text: Property passes when the contract is made, unless a different intention appears
options.explanation: That is the s. 20 rule for SPECIFIC goods in a deliverable state; s. 18 blocks it for unascertained goods.

options.text: No property in the goods is transferred to the buyer unless and until the goods are ascertained
options.explanation: Correct. Section 18 is an absolute bar which the parties' intention cannot override; only after ascertainment do the rules of intention in ss. 19 to 24 begin to operate.

options.text: Property passes when the price is paid in full
options.explanation: Payment is not the trigger anywhere in the Act; ascertainment followed by unconditional appropriation is.

options.text: Property passes when the buyer takes delivery, whatever the state of the goods
options.explanation: Delivery is a transfer of possession; it is appropriation with assent under s. 23 that passes the property.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 20 · Specific goods in a deliverable state
questions.stem: There is an unconditional contract for the sale of a specific tractor in a deliverable state. Both payment and delivery are postponed by agreement to a later date. Property in the tractor passes:

readLink.label: Read: Passing of property →

options.text: When the price is paid
options.explanation: Section 20 expressly says the postponement of payment is immaterial.

options.text: When the contract is made
options.explanation: Correct. Section 20 passes the property at the contract and adds that it is immaterial whether the time of payment of the price or the time of delivery, or both, is postponed.

options.text: When delivery is made
options.explanation: Section 20 expressly says the postponement of delivery is immaterial.

options.text: When both payment and delivery have taken place
options.explanation: This combines the two errors the section is drafted to exclude.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · ss. 21 and 22 · Deliverable state and weighing
questions.stem: A seller of specific goods in a deliverable state is bound to weigh them on his own weighbridge in order to ascertain the price. He weighs them on Monday but tells the buyer only on Thursday. Property passes:

readLink.label: Read: Passing of property →

options.text: On Thursday, when the buyer had notice of the weighing
options.explanation: Correct. Section 22 requires both that the act be done AND that the buyer have notice of it, so the later of the two events controls.

options.text: On Monday, when the weighing was completed
options.explanation: Doing the act is only half of s. 22; the section adds 'and the buyer has notice thereof'.

options.text: When the contract was made, the goods being specific and in a deliverable state
options.explanation: That would be s. 20, but s. 20 yields where the seller is bound to weigh the goods to ascertain the price.

options.text: Only on delivery of the goods to the buyer
options.explanation: Delivery is not the trigger; the Act separates the passing of property from the transfer of possession.

questions.stem: On 6 March 2026 a dealer delivers a set of surveying instruments to a buyer on sale or return, the contract providing that they are to be returned within 20 days if not approved. The buyer neither approves nor rejects, does nothing with the instruments, and simply keeps them. The property in the instruments passes to the buyer on:

readLink.label: Read: Sale or return, s. 24 →

options.text: 25 March 2026
options.explanation: This counts the day of delivery itself as day one; a period of days runs from and excludes the day of the trigger event.

options.text: 6 March 2026
options.explanation: Delivery on approval does not pass property at all; s. 24 sets out the three later events that do.

options.text: A reasonable time after 6 March 2026, to be fixed by the court
options.explanation: The reasonable-time limb of s. 24(b) applies only where NO time has been fixed. Here a period of 20 days was fixed.

options.text: 26 March 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Section 24(b) passes the property on the expiry of the fixed return period where the buyer retains the goods without giving notice of rejection: 20 days counted from and excluding 6 March ends on 26 March 2026.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 24(a) · Act adopting the transaction
questions.stem: A buyer who has received goods on sale or return pledges them with a moneylender well within the return period. The effect is that:

readLink.label: Read: Sale or return, s. 24 →

options.text: The property still passes only on the expiry of the return period
options.explanation: Section 24 passes the property on the EARLIEST of its triggers, and an act adopting the transaction comes before the expiry of time.

options.text: No property passes, since a pledge transfers only a special property in the goods
options.explanation: What matters is not what the pledge transfers to the pledgee but that the buyer has dealt with the goods as an owner.

options.text: The property passes to him at the moment of the pledge, as an act adopting the transaction
options.explanation: Correct. Pledging is an act adopting the transaction under s. 24(a); it is inconsistent with returning the goods, so the property passes at once and the return period becomes irrelevant.

options.text: The contract becomes void for want of the seller's consent to the pledge
options.explanation: The Act does not avoid the contract; it treats the buyer's conduct as an adoption and makes him liable for the price.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 25 · Reservation of the right of disposal
questions.stem: Goods are shipped and the bill of lading is made deliverable to the order of the seller. Under section 25(2) the seller is:

readLink.label: Read: Reservation of the right of disposal →

options.text: Deemed to have unconditionally appropriated the goods under s. 23(2)
options.explanation: Section 23(2) operates only where the seller does NOT reserve the right of disposal; the form of the bill of lading here shows that he did.

options.text: Deemed to have delivered the goods to the buyer under s. 39
options.explanation: Delivery to a carrier is prima facie delivery to the buyer, but that concerns possession and does not defeat an express reservation of the right of disposal.

options.text: Prima facie deemed to have reserved the right of disposal, so no property passes to the buyer on shipment
options.explanation: Correct. Section 25(2) creates that presumption where the bill of lading or railway receipt makes the goods deliverable to the order of the seller or his agent.

options.text: Bound to transfer the property because the goods have left his possession
options.explanation: Losing possession is not losing ownership; s. 25(1) expressly keeps the property in the seller notwithstanding delivery to a carrier.

questions.stem: On 2 June 2026 Farida buys from a dealer 150 identified bags of cement at ₹2,640 per bag, lying ready in his godown, delivery to be taken on 20 June and payment on 30 June. On 11 June the godown is destroyed by an accidental fire with no fault on either side. The amount Farida must pay is:

readLink.label: Read: Risk follows the property, s. 26 →

options.text: Nothing
options.explanation: This assumes the risk stayed with the seller because he still held the goods. Section 26 ties risk to property, not possession.
There is no rule sharing an accidental loss between the parties; the owner bears the whole of it.
This applies an arbitrary ten per cent abatement. The contract price is payable in full once the property, and with it the risk, has passed.
Correct. The goods were specific and in a deliverable state, so property passed on 2 June under s. 20 and the risk was Farida's under s. 26. She must pay the full price: 150 × ₹2,640 = ₹3,96,000.

questions.stem: Mohit obtains a camera from Nita by fraud and, before Nita rescinds, sells it to Omkar, who buys in good faith and without notice. Omkar:

readLink.label: Read: Transfer of title by a non-owner →

options.text: Gets no title, because Mohit obtained the camera by fraud
options.explanation: Fraud makes the contract voidable, not void, and s. 29 is drafted precisely for that gap between the fraud and the rescission.

options.text: Gets a good title, because the contract under which Mohit obtained the camera was voidable and had not been rescinded at the time of the sale
options.explanation: Correct. Section 29 protects a buyer in good faith without notice where the seller's own contract was voidable under s. 19 or 19A of the Contract Act and had not yet been avoided.

options.text: Gets a good title only if he has also taken delivery of the camera
options.explanation: Section 29 speaks of a buyer in good faith without notice; it does not add a delivery requirement.

options.text: Gets a good title only if Nita never rescinds at all
options.explanation: The timing that matters is rescission BEFORE the resale; a rescission afterwards cannot undo a title Omkar has already acquired.

questions.stem: A hirer under a hire-purchase agreement sells the goods to an innocent third party before paying the last instalment. The third party:

readLink.label: Read: Transfer of title by a non-owner →

options.text: Gets no title, because a hirer has only an OPTION to purchase and has not 'agreed to buy' within s. 30(2)
options.explanation: Correct. Section 30(2) protects transferees only from a person who has bought or agreed to buy; a hirer who may return the goods has not agreed to buy, so the owner recovers them.

options.text: Gets a good title under s. 30(2), the hirer being a buyer in possession with the owner's consent
options.explanation: This treats an option to purchase as an agreement to buy, which is the exact distinction the section turns on.

options.text: Gets a good title under the mercantile agent proviso to s. 27
options.explanation: A hirer is not a mercantile agent, and he was not in possession in that capacity.

options.text: Gets a good title if he pays the balance instalments to the owner
options.explanation: Paying the instalments may produce a settlement, but it is not a route to title under any exception in the Act.

questions.stem: The proviso to section 27 validates a sale by a mercantile agent only where, among other things:

readLink.label: Read: Transfer of title by a non-owner →

options.text: He was in possession of the goods or of a document of title with the owner's consent, acted in the ordinary course of business, and the buyer took in good faith without notice of the want of authority
options.explanation: Correct. All four limbs must be satisfied; drop any one and the sale falls back under the nemo dat rule in the main part of s. 27.

options.text: He was in possession of the goods, whether or not the owner consented
options.explanation: Consent of the owner is an express requirement; an agent who obtained possession without it cannot pass title.

options.text: He acted honestly, whatever the buyer knew
options.explanation: The proviso protects the BUYER's good faith and want of notice; the agent's own honesty is not the test.

options.text: The sale was for a price not less than the market value of the goods
options.explanation: The proviso says nothing about adequacy of price, though a grossly low price may be evidence that the buyer had notice.

questions.stem: Unless otherwise agreed, the expenses of and incidental to putting the goods into a deliverable state are borne by:

readLink.label: Read: Performance of the contract, s. 36 →

options.text: The buyer
options.explanation: This confuses the cost of putting goods into a deliverable state with the cost of taking delivery, which is indeed the buyer's.

options.text: The seller
options.explanation: Correct. Section 36(5) places the cost of putting the goods into a deliverable state on the seller; the cost of taking delivery falls on the buyer.

options.text: The party in whom the property in the goods is vested at the time
options.explanation: The Act allocates this expense by role, not by ownership; s. 26 uses ownership for RISK, not for delivery expenses.

options.text: The carrier, as part of the freight
options.explanation: Freight is a separate charge under the contract of carriage and has nothing to do with s. 36(5).

questions.stem: A seller delivers a quantity of goods LARGER than that contracted for. The buyer:

readLink.label: Read: Delivery of the wrong quantity, s. 37 →

options.text: Must accept the whole and pay for the excess at the market rate
options.explanation: There is no obligation to accept the excess, and if the whole is accepted the CONTRACT rate applies, not the market rate.

options.text: May accept the excess without paying for it, the seller having sent it voluntarily
options.explanation: Section 37(2) requires payment at the contract rate for everything accepted.

options.text: May accept the contract quantity and reject the rest, or reject the whole; and if he accepts the whole of the goods delivered he must pay for them at the contract rate
options.explanation: Correct. Section 37(2) gives both choices and fixes the price consequence of accepting the whole at the contract rate.

options.text: May reject only the excess and has no right to reject the whole
options.explanation: The right to reject the whole consignment is expressly given by s. 37(2).

questions.stem: Under section 42, the buyer is deemed to have accepted the goods in which of the following situations?

readLink.label: Read: Acceptance and the buyer's duties, s. 42 →

options.text: As soon as the goods are delivered to his premises
options.explanation: Delivery is not acceptance; s. 41 gives him a reasonable opportunity of examining the goods first.

options.text: When he pays the price in advance of delivery
options.explanation: Payment is not one of the three limbs of s. 42 and says nothing about conformity of the goods.

options.text: When he refuses the goods but declines to send them back to the seller
options.explanation: Section 43 says he need not return rejected goods; intimating refusal is enough, and doing so is the opposite of acceptance.

options.text: When he retains the goods after the lapse of a reasonable time without intimating to the seller that he has rejected them
options.explanation: Correct. This is the third limb of s. 42, alongside intimating acceptance and doing an act inconsistent with the seller's ownership.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the unpaid seller is correct?

readLink.label: Read: The unpaid seller and his rights →

options.text: A seller ceases to be unpaid once the buyer hands him a cheque, even if it is later dishonoured
options.explanation: Section 45(1)(b) restores his status the moment the instrument is dishonoured, because it was only conditional payment.

options.text: The unpaid seller's rights against the goods are lost as soon as the property passes to the buyer
options.explanation: Section 46 opens with the words 'notwithstanding that the property in the goods may have passed to the buyer'.

options.text: A tender of the price which the seller wrongfully refuses leaves him an unpaid seller
options.explanation: Section 45(1)(a) says 'paid or tendered', so a valid tender ends the seller's unpaid status just as payment would.

options.text: A seller who has received all but a small part of the price is still an unpaid seller with the full set of rights
options.explanation: Correct. Section 45(1)(a) requires that the WHOLE of the price be paid or tendered, so any shortfall keeps the seller unpaid.

questions.stem: Vinod, an unpaid seller who has lawfully exercised his lien over goods sold for ₹9,60,000, gives the buyer notice of his intention to resell. The buyer does not pay within a reasonable time and Vinod resells the goods for ₹10,35,000. The amount Vinod may keep out of the resale proceeds over and above the contract price is:

readLink.label: Read: Lien, stoppage in transit and resale →

options.explanation: Correct. Because notice of the intention to resell was given, the seller keeps the whole surplus: ₹10,35,000 − ₹9,60,000 = ₹75,000, and he could equally have recovered a deficiency as damages.

options.text: Nothing; the whole surplus belongs to the original buyer
options.explanation: That is the consequence where NO notice is given. Notice was given here, so the surplus is the seller's.
There is no rule sharing the surplus between seller and buyer; s. 54(2) gives it entirely to one side depending on notice.
This treats the whole resale price as a surplus and ignores the ₹9,60,000 contract price against which it must be set.

questions.stem: An unpaid seller who has exercised his right of stoppage in transit resells goods contracted at ₹5,40,000 for ₹5,94,000, WITHOUT giving the buyer any notice of his intention to resell. The goods are not perishable. The amount the original buyer may claim from the seller as the profit on the resale is:

readLink.label: Read: Lien, stoppage in transit and resale →

options.text: Nothing, because the resale was lawful and passed a good title
options.explanation: Section 54(3) does give the new buyer a good title even without notice, but title and the profit are separate questions; the profit follows the notice rule in s. 54(2).
This claims the entire resale price rather than the excess over the contract price.
Correct. Where no notice was given, s. 54(2) entitles the buyer to the profit on the resale and bars the seller from recovering damages: ₹5,94,000 − ₹5,40,000 = ₹54,000.
There is no sharing of the profit; the section gives it wholly to the buyer where notice was not given.

questions.stem: In a sale by auction, unless a different intention appears:

readLink.label: Read: Auction sale, s. 64 →

options.text: A bid, once made, is irrevocable and binds the bidder
options.explanation: This treats the bid as an acceptance. Section 64(2) expressly allows retraction until the sale is announced as complete.

options.text: A bidder may retract his bid at any time until the auctioneer announces the completion of the sale by the fall of the hammer or in other customary manner
options.explanation: Correct. Section 64(2) makes a bid an offer only, and the fall of the hammer the acceptance, so until then the bid may be withdrawn.

options.text: The seller may always bid at the auction to protect his interest
options.explanation: He may bid only where a right to bid has been expressly reserved (s. 64(3)); otherwise it is unlawful under s. 64(4).

options.text: Where several lots are put up, all the lots together form one contract of sale
options.explanation: Section 64(1) makes each lot prima facie the subject of a SEPARATE contract of sale.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · ss. 14 to 17 · Case: the cold-storage compressor
questions.case: Uma runs a cold storage for fruit at Sangli. On 4 January 2026 she tells Vikas Refrigeration, a dealer in industrial cooling equipment, that she needs a compressor 'able to hold 40 tonnes of produce at 2 degrees Celsius through a Maharashtra summer'. Vikas recommends the 'Shitalya IC-9' and sells her one for ₹6,20,000, the invoice describing it as an 'industrial compressor, 40-tonne duty'. A sample cooling coil had been shown to Uma at the showroom and the contract records that the coils supplied are to correspond with that sample. On delivery Uma inspects the machine externally and signs the delivery note. In April the compressor fails: its actual rated duty is 25 tonnes, the coils supplied are of a thinner gauge than the sample, and an internal valve carries a manufacturing flaw that no external inspection could have revealed. Vikas also turns out to have bought the compressor from a person who had himself taken it on hire-purchase and had not paid the last three instalments; the finance company reclaims the machine in May 2026.

readLink.label: Read: Implied conditions and warranties →

questions.stem: On the 25-tonne rated duty, the strongest ground on which Uma can proceed is:

options.text: Nothing, because she bought a specified article under its trade name
options.explanation: The proviso to s. 16(1) applies only where the buyer orders by trade name WITHOUT relying on the seller; here Vikas chose the model for her stated purpose.

options.text: Breach of the implied condition of fitness for a particular purpose, since she made her purpose known and relied on the seller's skill
options.explanation: Correct. She stated the 40-tonne, 2-degree requirement expressly, Vikas recommended the model, and compressors are goods he deals in — all three limbs of s. 16(1) are satisfied.

options.text: Breach of the implied warranty of quiet possession under s. 14(b)
options.explanation: Quiet possession concerns disturbance of the buyer's possession by someone with a better right, not the performance of the machine.

options.text: Breach of s. 16(3), an implied term annexed by usage of trade
options.explanation: No trade usage is pleaded on these facts; s. 16(3) needs proof of an established usage in the trade.

questions.stem: The invoice description 'industrial compressor, 40-tonne duty' gives Uma:

options.text: No independent ground, because a description in an invoice is not a contractual term
options.explanation: An invoice description that identifies what was sold forms part of the description for s. 15 purposes.

options.text: A ground only if the machine is also unmerchantable
options.explanation: Sections 15 and 16(2) are independent; goods can answer their description yet be unmerchantable, and vice versa.

options.text: A warranty only, since the shortfall in duty is collateral to the main purpose
options.explanation: Correspondence with description is a CONDITION under s. 15, not a warranty.

options.text: A separate ground under s. 15, the goods not corresponding with their description
options.explanation: Correct. Section 15 implies a condition that goods sold by description shall correspond with it, and a 25-tonne machine does not answer a 40-tonne description.

questions.stem: As to the flawed internal valve, Uma's external inspection at delivery:

options.text: Does not bar her, because the proviso to s. 16(2) excludes only defects which such examination ought to have revealed
options.explanation: Correct. The flaw was undetectable on any reasonable external inspection, so it is a latent defect and the condition of merchantable quality survives; s. 17(2)(c) gives her the same protection on the sample limb.

options.text: Bars her completely, since a buyer who examines goods accepts them as they are
options.explanation: Examination bars only the defects it ought to have revealed; it is not a blanket waiver.

options.text: Bars her unless she can show the seller knew of the flaw
options.explanation: Neither s. 16(2) nor its proviso turns on the seller's knowledge; the condition is strict.

options.text: Is irrelevant, because signing a delivery note is conclusive acceptance under s. 42
options.explanation: Signing for delivery is not one of the three limbs of s. 42, and s. 41 preserves a reasonable opportunity to examine.

questions.stem: When the finance company reclaims the compressor in May 2026, Uma's position is:

options.text: She keeps the machine, because she bought in good faith and without notice
options.explanation: Good faith alone is not a title. She would need to fall inside one of the exceptions to s. 27, and none applies to a sale by a hire-purchase hirer.

options.text: She recovers ₹6,20,000 less a fair charge for the use she has had
options.explanation: No allowance is made for use where the consideration has failed totally; she contracted for ownership and received none.

options.text: She recovers the entire ₹6,20,000 from Vikas for breach of the implied condition as to the right to sell, with no allowance for four months' use
options.explanation: Correct. The hirer could pass no title (he had only an option to buy, so s. 30(2) does not help), Vikas therefore had no right to sell, and the consideration has failed totally — Rowland v Divall.

options.text: She has only a claim for breach of the warranty of quiet possession, measured by her loss
options.explanation: Section 14(b) is also broken, but the primary breach is of the s. 14(a) CONDITION as to the right to sell, which returns the whole price.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · ss. 18 to 26, 57 · Case: the jaggery godown at Kolhapur
questions.case: Yashodha Traders holds jaggery in a Kolhapur godown. On 5 February 2026 it makes three contracts. (i) It sells to Praful 'the 300 bags marked lot YT-7 lying in Bay 2', ₹1,860 per bag, delivery and payment both due on 28 February. Nothing remains to be done to the bags. (ii) It sells to Qamar 500 quintals of jaggery at ₹4,100 per quintal out of an undivided heap of 1,200 quintals in Bay 5; nothing is weighed, marked or separated. (iii) It sends 20 tins of a new jaggery powder to Rekha, a retailer, 'on sale or return', no period for return being mentioned. On 14 February an accidental fire, with no fault on either side, destroys everything in Bays 2 and 5. Yashodha never delivers to Qamar; on 28 February 2026, the agreed delivery date and the date of breach, the market price of jaggery is ₹4,460 per quintal. Rekha still has the 20 tins, unopened and unsold, on 30 June 2026, and has said nothing to Yashodha.

readLink.label: Read: Passing of property →

questions.stem: As between Yashodha and Praful, the loss of the 300 bags falls on:

options.text: Yashodha, because the goods were still in its godown when the fire occurred
options.explanation: Possession is not the test. Section 26 ties risk to property, and the property had already passed.

options.text: Yashodha, because the price had not been paid on the date of the fire
options.explanation: Section 20 says in terms that postponement of the time of payment is immaterial to the passing of property.

options.text: Praful, because property in the specific bags passed on 5 February and risk follows property
options.explanation: Correct. The bags were specific and in a deliverable state under an unconditional contract, so s. 20 passed the property at once, and s. 26 puts the risk on the owner even though delivery and payment were postponed.

options.text: Both equally, the loss being accidental and neither party at fault
options.explanation: The Act does not share an accidental loss; it places it wholly on whoever owned the goods.

questions.stem: As between Yashodha and Qamar, the correct analysis of the 500 quintals is:

options.text: Property never passed because the goods were unascertained, so the loss is Yashodha's and the contract is not avoided
options.explanation: Correct. Section 18 blocks the passing of property until ascertainment, so the risk stayed with the seller; and s. 8 cannot avoid the agreement because it applies only to SPECIFIC goods.

options.text: The agreement is avoided under s. 8, the goods having perished without fault
options.explanation: Section 8 requires specific goods. An undivided part of a bulk is unascertained, so the section has no application.

options.text: Property passed on the making of the contract under s. 20, so Qamar bears the loss
options.explanation: Section 20 applies to specific goods in a deliverable state; nothing here was identified and agreed upon.

options.text: The contract is void under s. 7, the subject matter having been destroyed
options.explanation: Section 7 deals with goods that had perished BEFORE the contract was made, and again only specific goods.

questions.stem: The damages Qamar may recover from Yashodha for non-delivery of the 500 quintals amount to:

options.explanation: This is the contract value of the undelivered goods, 500 × ₹4,100, not the loss Qamar has suffered.
This is the market value of the goods, 500 × ₹4,460; Qamar must still pay a price for substitute goods, so only the excess is his loss.

options.text: Nothing, because the goods were destroyed in an accidental fire
options.explanation: The fire destroys generic goods but not the obligation; the market in jaggery has not perished, so Yashodha must source elsewhere or pay damages.
Correct. The measure is the difference between the market price on the date of breach and the contract price, multiplied by the quantity: (₹4,460 − ₹4,100) × 500 = ₹1,80,000.

questions.stem: As to the 20 tins with Rekha on 30 June 2026:

options.text: Property remains with Yashodha until Rekha signifies her approval
options.explanation: This reads only limb (a) of s. 24 and ignores limb (b), which operates precisely where the buyer says nothing.

options.text: Property has passed to Rekha on the expiry of a reasonable time, no period for return having been fixed
options.explanation: Correct. Section 24(b) passes the property on the expiry of a reasonable time where none is fixed and the buyer retains the goods without giving notice of rejection; four and a half months of silence is plainly beyond it.

options.text: Property passed when the tins were delivered on 5 February
options.explanation: Goods delivered on approval do not pass property on delivery; that is the whole point of a sale-or-return arrangement.

options.text: The contract is void for uncertainty because no return period was fixed
options.explanation: Section 24(b) supplies a reasonable time in exactly that situation, so there is no uncertainty to avoid the contract.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · ss. 45 to 54 · Case: the lathes stopped on the Trichy road
questions.case: Balaji Tools sells six lathes to Chola Engineering for ₹7,50,000, payment due 30 days after delivery. The lathes leave Balaji's works by lorry on 3 June 2026 for Chola's plant at Trichy. On 6 June, while the lorry is still on the road and Chola has taken delivery of nothing, Balaji learns that Chola has stopped paying its suppliers and that three of its cheques have bounced; no insolvency petition has been filed against Chola. Balaji gives written notice to the transport company, which returns the lathes to Balaji's works on 8 June at a redelivery cost of ₹22,000. On 10 June Balaji writes to Chola: 'Pay the price within ten days or the lathes will be resold.' Chola pays nothing. On 24 June 2026 Balaji resells all six lathes to Kaveri Fabricators, who buys in good faith, for ₹6,90,000.

readLink.label: Read: The unpaid seller and his rights →

questions.stem: The right Balaji exercised on 6 June, and its validity, are:

options.text: A lien under s. 47, and it is valid because the price was unpaid
options.explanation: A lien depends on the seller being in POSSESSION. Balaji had handed the lathes to a carrier, which ends the lien under s. 49(1)(a).

options.text: Stoppage in transit, but it is invalid because Chola has not been adjudged insolvent
options.explanation: Section 2(8) requires only that the buyer has ceased to pay his debts in the ordinary course of business or cannot pay them as they become due, whether adjudged or not.

options.text: Stoppage in transit, but it is invalid because notice was given to the carrier rather than by taking actual possession
options.explanation: Section 52(1) permits either mode: taking actual possession OR giving notice of the claim to the carrier or bailee.

options.text: Stoppage in transit, and it is valid, because Chola had ceased to pay its debts in the ordinary course of business and the goods had not yet been delivered
options.explanation: Correct. The lien ended when the goods went to a carrier without a reservation of disposal (s. 49(1)(a)); s. 50 then applies, and s. 2(8) defines insolvency commercially, so no adjudication is needed while the goods remain in transit under s. 51.

questions.stem: The amount Balaji may recover from Chola as the loss occasioned by the resale is:

options.explanation: This adds the ₹22,000 redelivery expense, which s. 52(2) expressly places on the seller who exercises stoppage in transit.

Correct. Notice of the intention to resell was given and a reasonable time allowed, so s. 54(2) lets Balaji recover the deficiency: ₹7,50,000 − ₹6,90,000 = ₹60,000. The ₹22,000 redelivery cost is not part of this figure because s. 52(2) puts the expenses of redelivery on the seller.

options.text: Nothing, because a resale by an unpaid seller rescinds the contract
options.explanation: A resale after lien or stoppage does not rescind the contract; s. 54(1) says so, and only an express reserved right of resale under s. 54(4) has that effect.
This is the resale price, not the shortfall against the original contract price.

questions.stem: Kaveri Fabricators' title to the six lathes, and the effect of the resale on the original contract, are:
questions.topic: Ch 3 · ss. 54(1), 54(3) · Title of the new buyer

options.text: Kaveri gets a good title as against Chola under s. 54(3), and the original contract was not rescinded by the exercise of stoppage in transit
options.explanation: Correct. Section 54(3) protects the new buyer whether or not notice of the resale was given, and s. 54(1) makes clear that a lien or stoppage does not rescind the contract of sale.

options.text: Kaveri gets no title, because the property in the lathes had already passed to Chola
options.explanation: Section 54(3) is an express statutory exception to nemo dat for a resale by an unpaid seller who has exercised lien or stoppage.

options.text: Kaveri gets a good title only because notice of the intended resale had been given to Chola
options.explanation: Notice governs who keeps the profit and whether damages can be recovered; s. 54(3) protects the new buyer's title even without notice.

options.text: Kaveri gets a good title and the original contract stood rescinded from 6 June
options.explanation: The title point is right but the rescission point is wrong: s. 54(1) says the contract is not rescinded by the mere exercise of a lien or stoppage in transit.

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 4 · Sale and agreement to sell
questions.stem: Distinguish between a 'sale' and an 'agreement to sell' under the Sale of Goods Act 1930, and state the consequences that follow from the distinction. (6 marks)

readLink.label: Read: Sale and agreement to sell, s. 4 →

skeleton.point: Definitions: a contract of sale is one whereby the seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods for a price; where property is transferred at the time of the contract it is a SALE, and where the transfer is to take place at a future time or subject to a condition it is an AGREEMENT TO SELL
An agreement to sell becomes a sale when the time elapses or the conditions are fulfilled subject to which the property is to be transferred
Nature: a sale is an executed contract creating a right in rem; an agreement to sell is executory and creates a right in personam only
Risk: in a sale the risk is on the buyer even if the goods are still with the seller; in an agreement to sell it remains with the seller even if the goods are with the buyer

Insolvency: on the seller's insolvency a buyer who has paid can claim the goods themselves under a sale but only a dividend under an agreement to sell; on the buyer's insolvency the seller under an agreement to sell may refuse delivery unless paid in full

Remedies and resale: under a sale the seller may sue for the price and a resale to a third party passes no title; under an agreement to sell the seller may sue only for damages for non-acceptance and a resale passes a good title to the third party

questions.topic: Ch 3 · ss. 14 to 17 · Implied conditions and warranties
questions.stem: State the implied conditions and implied warranties in a contract for the sale of goods, indicating in each case the section under which they arise. (6 marks)

readLink.label: Read: Implied conditions and warranties →

skeleton.point: Implied condition as to title: in a sale, that the seller has a right to sell the goods; in an agreement to sell, that he will have such a right at the time the property is to pass
Implied condition that goods sold by description shall correspond with the description; and where the sale is by sample as well as by description, the bulk must answer both

Implied condition of fitness for the buyer's particular purpose where the purpose is made known expressly or by implication, the buyer relies on the seller's skill or judgment, and the goods are of a description the seller supplies in the course of business; excluded by the proviso for a specified article bought under its patent or trade name
Implied condition of merchantable quality on a sale by description by a dealer in such goods, subject to the proviso excluding defects which the buyer's actual examination ought to have revealed

Implied conditions on a sale by sample: bulk to correspond with the sample in quality, a reasonable opportunity of comparing bulk with sample, and freedom from latent defects rendering the goods unmerchantable

The two implied WARRANTIES: quiet possession, and freedom from any charge or encumbrance in favour of a third party not declared or known to the buyer; a condition or warranty may also be annexed by usage of trade, and an express term does not negative an implied one unless inconsistent

questions.stem: Explain the doctrine of caveat emptor and state its exceptions under the Sale of Goods Act 1930. (5 marks)

readLink.label: Read: Caveat emptor and its exceptions →

skeleton.point: Statement of the doctrine: subject to the Act and any other law in force there is no implied condition or warranty as to the quality or fitness for any particular purpose of goods supplied under a contract of sale; the buyer must rely on his own skill and judgment (Ward v Hobbs)
Exception 1: fitness for the buyer's particular purpose where the purpose is made known and the buyer relies on the seller's skill or judgment
Exception 2: merchantable quality where goods are bought by description from a seller who deals in goods of that description
Exception 3: a condition or warranty annexed by the usage of trade
Exceptions 4 and 5: sale by sample, where the three conditions in s. 17 apply; and sale by sample as well as by description, where the goods must answer both

Exception 6: fraud, misrepresentation or active concealment of a defect by the seller; and note that where the buyer orders a specified article under its patent or trade name without relying on the seller, caveat emptor continues to apply
skeleton.citation: s. 16(1) proviso; Contract Act ss. 17 to 19

questions.topic: Ch 3 · ss. 18 to 24 · Passing of property
questions.stem: State the rules for ascertaining when the property in goods passes from the seller to the buyer, dealing separately with specific goods and unascertained goods. (6 marks)

readLink.label: Read: Passing of property →

skeleton.point: Master rule: in a contract for the sale of specific or ascertained goods the property passes when the parties intend it to pass, regard being had to the terms of the contract, the conduct of the parties and the circumstances; ss. 20 to 24 are only rules for ascertaining that intention
Specific goods in a deliverable state under an unconditional contract: property passes when the contract is made, and postponement of the time of payment or of delivery, or both, is immaterial
Specific goods which the seller is bound to put into a deliverable state: property passes when that is done AND the buyer has notice thereof
Specific goods in a deliverable state which the seller must weigh, measure or test to ascertain the price: property passes when that act is done AND the buyer has notice thereof

Unascertained goods: no property passes unless and until the goods are ascertained; thereafter property passes on an unconditional appropriation of goods of the contract description in a deliverable state by one party with the assent of the other, and delivery to a carrier without reserving the right of disposal is deemed such an appropriation

Goods sent on approval or on sale or return: property passes on approval or acceptance, or on any act adopting the transaction, or on the expiry of the fixed time for return, or of a reasonable time where none is fixed, the goods being retained without notice of rejection

questions.topic: Ch 3 · s. 27 · Transfer of title by non-owners
questions.stem: 'No one can give a better title than he himself has.' Explain this rule and state the exceptions to it under the Sale of Goods Act 1930. (6 marks)

readLink.label: Read: Transfer of title by a non-owner →

skeleton.point: The rule: where goods are sold by a person who is not the owner and who does not sell them under the authority or with the consent of the owner, the buyer acquires no better title than the seller had, unless the owner is by his conduct precluded from denying the seller's authority to sell (nemo dat quod non habet)
Exception 1, estoppel: where the owner by his conduct, words or omission leads the buyer to believe that the seller had authority to sell

Exception 2, sale by a mercantile agent in possession of the goods or documents of title with the owner's consent, acting in the ordinary course of business, to a buyer in good faith without notice of the want of authority
Exception 3, sale by one of several joint owners who has sole possession by permission of the others, to a buyer in good faith without notice

Exception 4, sale by a person in possession under a contract voidable for coercion, undue influence, fraud or misrepresentation, where the contract has not been rescinded at the time of the sale and the buyer takes in good faith without notice of the defect

Exceptions 5 and 6, sale by a seller who continues in possession after a sale, and sale by a buyer who has bought or agreed to buy and is in possession with the seller's consent, in each case to a transferee in good faith without notice

Exceptions 7 to 9, resale by an unpaid seller who has exercised lien or stoppage in transit; sale by a finder of goods; and sale by a pawnee on default, together with sales under statutory powers or an order of court

questions.stem: Who is an 'unpaid seller'? State his rights against the goods and against the buyer, and explain when the right of lien and the right of stoppage in transit are lost. (7 marks)

readLink.label: Read: The unpaid seller and his rights →

skeleton.point: Definition: a seller is unpaid when the whole of the price has not been paid or tendered, or when a negotiable instrument received as conditional payment has been dishonoured; the term includes any person in the position of a seller, such as an agent to whom the bill of lading has been indorsed

Rights against the goods: a lien on the goods for the price while in possession; a right of stopping the goods in transit on the buyer's insolvency after possession has been parted with; a right of resale as limited by the Act; and, where the property has not passed, a right of withholding delivery co-extensive with lien and stoppage
Rights against the buyer personally: suit for the price, suit for damages for non-acceptance, suit for interest and special damages, and the right to treat an anticipatory repudiation as a breach

The lien arises in three cases only: goods sold without any stipulation as to credit; goods sold on credit where the term of credit has expired; and the buyer becoming insolvent; and it may be exercised even though the seller holds the goods as agent or bailee for the buyer

The lien is lost by delivering the goods to a carrier or other bailee for transmission to the buyer without reserving the right of disposal, by the buyer or his agent lawfully obtaining possession, or by waiver; it is not lost merely by obtaining a decree for the price

Stoppage in transit requires the buyer's insolvency and goods still in transit; transit ends when the buyer or his agent takes delivery, when the carrier acknowledges holding the goods on the buyer's behalf after arrival, or when the carrier wrongfully refuses to deliver to the buyer

questions.stem: State the rules governing a sale by auction under section 64 of the Sale of Goods Act 1930. (4 marks)

readLink.label: Read: Auction sale, s. 64 →

skeleton.point: Where goods are put up for sale in lots, each lot is prima facie deemed to be the subject of a separate contract of sale

The sale is complete when the auctioneer announces its completion by the fall of the hammer or in other customary manner, and until then any bidder may retract his bid; a bid is therefore an offer only
A right to bid may be reserved expressly by or on behalf of the seller, and only where it is so reserved may the seller or one person on his behalf bid at the auction

Where the sale is not notified to be subject to a right to bid on behalf of the seller, it is unlawful for the seller to bid or to employ any person to bid, or for the auctioneer knowingly to take such a bid, and any sale contravening this rule may be treated as fraudulent by the buyer
The sale may be notified to be subject to a reserved or upset price; and if the seller makes use of pretended bidding to raise the price, the sale is voidable at the option of the buyer
